true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `downsize` definition overrides the 4-arg version

Ruby has no method overloading. The new `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` silently replaces the earlier `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`. Existing callers that pass a width and a height will now have `max_height` treated as `opts`. That either raises (`opts[:allow_animation]` called on an Integer) or produces a wrong dimensions string. Avatar and thumbnail downsizing elsewhere breaks as a result.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client hardcodes a 10MB limit for all uploads, ignoring max_attachment_size_kb

The client-side check previously used `max_<type>_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to 10MB for attachments as well, so the attachment size setting is no longer enforced or reported on the client. Users get wrong error messages, and the limit mismatches the configured server limit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and may not shrink file

The return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is ignored. If convert fails, the loop simply retries. After 5 attempts the file can still be over the limit, and the upload proceeds anyway. Resizing to 80% of dimensions also does not guarantee the byte size drops, for example with PNG or with quality changes. Running convert on the same path as both input and output can also corrupt the file on failure.

Downsizing uses the tempfile path, whose extension may not match

The animated-GIF check uses `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` on the tempfile path. Rack and download tempfiles usually lack the original extension, so animated GIFs are processed by convert using only frame `[0]`. This silently destroys the animation even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled.

Hardcoded 10MB download limit for API URL uploads

Downloads by URL are now capped at a hardcoded 10MB instead of a setting. Attachments fetched this way bypass the configured limits until `Upload.create_for` runs, and admins cannot tune the cap.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes on nil host

The callback calls `self.host.sub!` with no nil check. If `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` is missing, or a record is built without a host, this raises NoMethodError and the request returns a 500 instead of a validation error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unknown id causes NoMethodError instead of 404

`update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first`, which returns nil for an unknown id. They then call methods on that nil, producing a 500 error. Use `find` (or an equivalent) so a missing record returns a 404.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host lookup lowercases the column but not the input

`record_for_host` compares `lower(host)` against `uri.host` without downcasing the input. The model does not normalize case on save, so a stored host like 'Example.com' only matches a referer if the referer's hostname is already lowercase. A mixed-case referer or embed URL is rejected even though hostnames are case-insensitive. Downcase the input value before querying.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped interpolation of host values into SQL

Each old host value is interpolated directly into an INSERT statement without quoting. A value containing a quote breaks the migration and can inject SQL. The values are also not stripped or normalized, so entries with http://, a path, or trailing whitespace/CR are migrated as-is and will never match `host_allowed?`. Existing embeds would silently stop working after the upgrade.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents swapped

category_fabricator.rb now defines `:embeddable_host`, while embeddable_host_fabricator.rb defines the category fabricators. The tests still work, but the file names are misleading for anyone looking for either fabricator.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped interpolation of host values into SQL

Each old host value is interpolated directly into an INSERT statement without quoting. A value containing a quote breaks the migration and can inject SQL. The values are also not stripped or normalized, so entries with http://, a path, or trailing whitespace/CR are migrated as-is and will never match `host_allowed?`. Existing embeds would silently stop working after the upgrade.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category is not set

`execute(...)[0]['id']` assumes the join query returns a row. On sites with no `embed_category` setting, or one that names no existing category, `[0]` is nil and the migration raises NoMethodError, which blocks the deploy. The same problem exists at line 15 when `uncategorized_category_id` has no row in site_settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Displayed category is wrong when none is selected

If no category is chosen, `categoryId` is null and the server saves the uncategorized category. The client instead sets `host.category` from `findById(null)`, so the row shows a blank category badge rather than the category the server actually stored.

Validation rejects localhost and long TLDs

The format regex requires a TLD of 2–5 letters. It rejects hosts such as `localhost`, IP addresses, and longer TLDs (e.g. .museum, .technology). Values the old setting allowed, possibly brought over by the migration, can no longer be saved.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil TopicUser causes 500 on unsubscribe

`TopicUser.find_by` returns nil when the user has no topic_users row, for example a user notified through a mention or a category watch who never visited the topic. The next line calls `tu.notification_level` on nil and raises NoMethodError. Create the record if it is missing, or use `TopicUser.change`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Added explicit render :show may double-render

This change adds `render :show` inside `format.html` in `perform_show_response`. `show` then calls `canonical_url` after `perform_show_response`. Other callers may already rely on implicit rendering, so the change risks a DoubleRenderError. It also alters existing `show` behavior even though only `unsubscribe` needed it.

Client route fetches normal topic view, not unsubscribe endpoint

The client route loads the topic through `PostStream.loadTopicView`, which calls the normal topic JSON endpoint and never hits `/unsubscribe`. When a user navigates to this route inside the app, no unsubscribe happens, yet the page still says "You will stop receiving notifications".

Direct save bypasses TopicUser.change side effects

`tu.save!` skips what `TopicUser.change` normally does. It does not set `notifications_reason_id` or `notifications_changed_at`, and it does not publish the MessageBus notification_level_change. As a result, open clients do not update, and later auto-tracking can override the user's explicit choice because the reason stays nil.

No tests for the unsubscribe controller action

The new `TopicsController#unsubscribe` action has no specs. Untested paths include the regular-to-muted transition, the redirect when the slug does not match, and the case where no TopicUser row exists, which currently crashes.

No visibility check before modifying TopicUser

`TopicView.new` in the unsubscribe action is called without the slug-redirect handling used in `show`. The action then creates or modifies state for the topic, so the guard enforced by TopicView is the only protection. There is also no handling for a missing topic: `@topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url` is used when the slug is blank.

Repeated GET toggles state and mutates on GET

The unsubscribe action changes state on a GET request. A user whose level is already regular gets set to muted. Every revisit of the link, a link prefetch, or an email scanner fetching the URL lowers the level further or changes it unexpectedly. A state-changing GET is also CSRF-able: any third-party page can embed the URL and change a logged-in user's notification level.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match counter updated with racy read-modify-write during validation

`should_block?` loads the record, increments `match_count` in Ruby and saves it. Concurrent requests for the same address lose increments. It also writes to the database on every `valid?` call, so the count is inflated: `UsersController#create` validates twice (once in `user.valid?`, once in `save`). An atomic `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1')` would avoid the race.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` runs `where(email: value)` on the raw value. At validation time the user's email has not been downcased or normalized, so `Bad@Spammers.org` will not match a stored `bad@spammers.org`. A blocked address can register just by changing the letter case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Any email error permanently rejects the address client-side

The client records the email as rejected on any email error, including a transient one such as a uniqueness conflict. That address then can never be resubmitted from the form. The reason shown is also the generic "invalid" message, not the server's actual error.

Whitelist/blacklist behavior moved without tests

The domain whitelist/blacklist logic was moved out of `User` into `EmailValidator`, but the new spec only covers the blocked-email path. The moved logic has no coverage. There is also no test that a whitelist or blacklist failure skips the blocked-email check.

rejectedEmails array is shared across controller instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared in the prototype passed to `extend`, so every instance shares the same array. Rejected emails therefore persist across modal reopenings and across controller instances instead of being per-instance state. It should be initialized in `init`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped URL injected into raw HTML post

The feed or remote URL is interpolated directly into `<a href='#{url}'>` without escaping. Posts using cook_method raw_html skip sanitization, so a URL containing `'` or `<` produces stored XSS. Imported feed content as a whole is also rendered with `raw post.cooked` and never sanitized, so a compromised feed source can inject scripts.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil content crashes feed poll

`i.content.scrub` raises NoMethodError for RSS items that have no content (only a description), which aborts the whole poll. `scrub` also requires Ruby 2.1.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer interpolated unescaped into inline JS

Line 11 writes `request.referer` into a JS string literal with `<%= %>`. That helper HTML-escapes but does not JS-escape, so a backslash or other JS-significant character in an attacker-chosen referer can break out of the literal. The host check only validates the host part, and the path and query of the referer are still attacker-controlled. The target origin should be built from the configured embeddable_host instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate:
Every embed miss triggers a full feed poll

Each retrieve for an unknown URL synchronously polls and imports the entire feed. Staff requests bypass throttling, so this can cause repeated heavy fetches.

Mutates caller's string; fails on frozen strings

`contents <<` modifies the argument in place. Callers passing literals or frozen strings, such as `doc.content`, may get errors. The caller's data is also silently altered.

Race creating duplicate embeds

Two concurrent imports of the same URL can both see no existing embed. Both then create a topic, and the second `TopicEmbed.create!` raises on the unique index. Because creator.create runs inside the transaction, this rolls back with an exception that is not handled.

Spec expects TopicRetriever but controller enqueues a job

In the test environment queue_jobs is false, so `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic)` runs the job inline. That job calls `TopicRetriever.new(url, no_throttle: ...)` and the stub returns a bare mock. The spec only works through this indirect path. It does not check that the job is enqueued with the right args.

Start discussion branch unreachable

@topic_view is only set when a topic exists, and that topic always has at least the imported post. The 'start_discussion' branch therefore never shows, even when a topic has no replies.

open(url) with untrusted input allows command execution/SSRF

Kernel#open from open-uri is called on the URL. A value starting with '|' executes a shell command. The disqus import passes thread links straight from the XML file, and the URL is not validated as http before this call. Use URI.parse(url).open or an HTTP client, and validate the scheme first.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits invalid legacy values for old-box syntax

The align-items mixin passes values like `flex-start`, `flex-end` and `baseline` straight to `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`. Those legacy properties expect `start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline` and `stretch`, so `flex-start`/`flex-end` produce invalid declarations. The mixin also emits `-ms-align-items`, which is not a real property.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

false_positives.candidate:
Floats inside the new flex container are ignored

`.small-action` is now a flex container, but its children still use `float: left` (`.topic-avatar`) and `float: right` (the button). Floats are ignored on flex items, so the button no longer goes to the right and instead sits right after the description. `clear: both` is also meaningless here.

Legacy box-ordinal-group ordering inconsistent across flex items

`.panel` gets `order(3)` and `.extra-info-wrapper` gets `order(2)`, but the other flex children (title/logo) have no order set. In the old -webkit-box/-moz-box model, `box-ordinal-group` defaults to 1, while modern `order` defaults to 0. The two models therefore lay the items out differently. Also, the `.panel` children (`.login-button`, `.icons`) still use floats inside the now-flex row, which is fragile.

Removing .title float may break header layout in other stylesheets

The `.title { float: left; }` rule was removed, and `.contents` now relies on flexbox. In browsers that only support the legacy box model, `margin-left: auto` on `.panel` does not push it right. The panel would then render adjacent to the title instead of right-aligned, with no float fallback left in place.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name missing `?` so website_name leaks for restricted TL0 users

ActiveModel::Serializers only checks filter methods that end in `?`, so `include_website_name` is never called and `website_name` is always serialized. The field is also not listed in `untrusted_attributes`. As a result, the website host and path of a TL0 user is exposed to anonymous viewers, even though `website` itself is hidden from them. The method should be renamed to `include_website_name?` and apply the same `restrict_user_fields?` check (or `website_name` added to `untrusted_attributes`). The TL0 spec's attribute list should also cover `website_name`.

false_positives.candidate:
Hostnames compared case-sensitively

URI#host preserves the case of the input, so a website like `http://Example.com/user` will not match a Discourse host of `example.com`. Both hosts should be downcased before comparison.

Same-level subdomain comparison treats unrelated domains as same site

When both hosts have the same number of labels (more than 2), the code compares everything after the first label. For a two-part public suffix this goes wrong: with discourse host `forum.co.uk` and website `evil.co.uk`, both reduce to `co.uk` and are judged to be the same site. The full path of a third-party site is then shown. The logic has no notion of the registrable domain.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages off by one when count is a multiple of limit

`totalPages` is computed as `floor(user_count/limit)+1`, so 50 members with a limit of 50 shows 2 pages. Because `showingLast` compares `currentPage` with this inflated total, the next button stays enabled on the last real page. Clicking it sets offset to `user_count` and fetches an empty member list. Use `Math.ceil(user_count/limit)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test uses wrong HTTP verb

The test "cannot remove members from automatic groups" sends `xhr :put` to `remove_member`, but the route is DELETE. It therefore does not exercise the real routed request.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

totalPages off by one when count is a multiple of limit

`totalPages` is computed as `floor(user_count/limit)+1`, so 50 members with a limit of 50 shows 2 pages. Because `showingLast` compares `currentPage` with this inflated total, the next button stays enabled on the last real page. Clicking it sets offset to `user_count` and fetches an empty member list. true_positives.golden_comment: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined
true_positives.matched_candidate:
findMembers returns undefined instead of a promise

When the group name is empty, `findMembers` now returns `undefined` instead of a resolved promise. The `next`/`previous` actions return its result, so any caller that chains `.then()` on it will throw.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded limit on public members endpoint

The public `members` endpoint takes `limit` straight from the request with no maximum. Any user can request e.g. `limit=1000000` on a large automatic group and force a huge query and serialization. Negative `limit`/`offset` values are not rejected either. Clamp both values to a sane range.

`automatic` not resolved in item view context

Inside the `each ... itemView` the template context is the item view, so `automatic` likely does not resolve to the group's property. The remove link may then be shown for automatic groups; the server rejects the request with a 422, so the user sees a broken action.

addMembers has no error handling and doesn't clear input

`addMembers` has no failure handler, so failed additions (e.g. the 422 for automatic groups) fail silently with no message to the admin. The username input is also never cleared after a successful add (noted by the TODO), so it can be resubmitted by accident.

create ignores alias_level

The client sends `alias_level` in `asJSON` when creating a group, but `create` never assigns `params[:alias_level]`. Any alias level chosen when creating a new group is silently dropped and the group gets the default.

remove_member bypasses group.remove

`remove_member` calls `group.users.delete(user_id)` with a raw id instead of the existing `group.remove(user)` API used elsewhere. Removing by integer id on a has_many through association is unreliable, and any callbacks or side effects in `group.remove` are skipped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback list may contain a locale string alongside its symbol

The current locale is passed through unchanged while the site default is converted to a symbol. If the locale arrives as a string (for example 'en'), uniq does not collapse it with :en. The same locale is then looked up twice, and ensure_loaded! tracks both forms.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded outside controller requests

translate only loads config.locale. The fallback locales are loaded only by I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale. Jobs, mailers, rake tasks and any other non-controller code never load the site-default or :en translations. In those contexts, fallback lookups to unloaded locales return 'translation missing'.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, which depends on site default locale

Cached translations are keyed only by key, locale and backend. With fallbacks, the result for a missing key now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale. When the default locale changes, or differs between multisite sites in the same process, the LRU cache keeps serving stale or wrong-site fallback strings.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
UsernameForm calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no argument

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method defined, in `UsernamePasswordForm`, takes a `UserModel` parameter, so this code will not compile. It should pass `context.getUser()`, or a no-argument overload should be added.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login

The new helper returns true only when `user != null`. Before this change, passkeys were set up only when the user was not yet identified. In `authenticate()` and `challenge()` the call is now `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`. On a fresh login the user is null, so `fillContextForm` is never called and the conditional passkey UI is gone. That breaks the main passkeys login path, which several existing tests expect to show the webauth form before the username is entered. The condition looks inverted, or the null check should simply be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset slicing on Django QuerySet raises error

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the paginator slices the queryset with a negative start index (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError` ("Negative indexing is not supported"). Any request whose cursor has a negative offset therefore gets an unhandled exception and a 500 response. The code comment saying the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically" is wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible AttributeError when member is None

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated even when the requester has no membership, for example a superuser or staff user accessing the org, in which case `member` can be None. The `or` short-circuits only when `is_superuser` is true, so other non-member users with audit access (such as staff) crash with `AttributeError` before the check completes.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime keys

`get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on the raw attribute value, and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw number. The audit-log endpoint orders this paginator by `-datetime`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError` whenever there are results. Cursor values would also be compared against the datetime column as plain numbers, which is wrong. The optimized path fails for any non-empty result set; it should use the DateTimePaginator conversion logic.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator passes negative offsets through for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` clamps only next cursors. A user-supplied prev cursor such as `1:-5:1` slices the queryset with a negative index, which raises an error and returns a 500. This affects every BasePaginator subclass across the API, not only the new audit-log path.

No tests for new paginator or endpoint branch

The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, a new endpoint branch, and changes BasePaginator offset handling, but includes no tests. The datetime-key crash and the negative-slice errors would have been caught by basic tests.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets passed to Django queryset slicing raise errors

When advanced features are enabled and cursor.offset < 0, the code calls queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise ValueError/AssertionError, so a crafted cursor turns into a 500. The comment saying "the ORM handles negative slicing automatically" is false.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now passes negative offsets through for prev cursors

For prev cursors, start_offset is set to the raw offset with no clamping. Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets, so a user-supplied cursor like '123:-5:1' leads to negative queryset slicing on every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. That raises an exception and returns a 500. The previous behaviour also passed the offset through, but the new comment claims this is safe, which it is not; the offset should be clamped or rejected.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime keys

get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on the key value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw number. The audit log endpoint orders this paginator by `datetime`, so math.floor on a datetime raises TypeError and the cursor number is compared against a datetime column. true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member may be None

For superusers or staff who are not members of the organization, organization_context.member is None. Because `or` is evaluated left to right, superusers short-circuit and are fine. However, any non-superuser request without a membership raises AttributeError on `.has_global_access`, and that happens even when optimized_pagination was not requested.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for eviction behavior

The new 1000-span eviction in add-buffer.lua is not covered by any test, so there is nothing verifying the cap or which spans are dropped.

__reduce__ passes redis_ttl positionally into segment_page_size

The pickled SpansBuffer is rebuilt with (shards, timeout, root_timeout, redis_ttl). The fourth positional parameter of __init__ is segment_page_size, so after unpickling in multiprocessing workers, redis_ttl lands in segment_page_size and the real TTL resets to its default.

span_count can be stale after the second zunionstore is skipped

span_count is set from the first union. If the second union is skipped, the count is correct. If the parent union runs, the count is overwritten, which is fine. However, when neither union runs, the count falls back to zcard, so this path is okay. The real problem is that the eviction cap is a hardcoded 1000 spans, while max_segment_spans=1001 in Python is now unused. Eviction with zpopmin removes the spans with the earliest end timestamps, which can include the root span, so segments silently lose data with no metric or log.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Python hash() in shared cache key

The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(...))` and is stored in a shared cache. Hashing a tuple of ints is stable across processes today, but it can collide, and two different project sets that collide would read each other's eligibility result. Use a deterministic join of the sorted IDs or a digest such as md5 instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling check uses outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is passed the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`. During the dashboard split flow, `_get_event_stats` is called with `discover` for errors-only queries and with the original dataset for other queries. The upsampling decision is still made from the request's top-level dataset. As a result, upsampling can be applied to the wrong dataset, or skipped for the error split queries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule committed

A gitlink named `sentry-repo` pointing at the base commit has been added to the repository. It appears to be an accidental commit with no purpose in this change, and it will break clones and CI for anyone who initializes submodules. Remove it.

Eligibility cache defeats allowlist changes, and the invalidation helper is never called

The allowlist result is cached for 60 seconds. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere, so allowlist changes take up to 60 seconds to apply. The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the configuration is read fresh each time, which the cache contradicts. Separately, the comment justifies the cache as avoiding an expensive option lookup, but `options.get` is already cached locally, so the extra cache round-trip likely makes things slower, not faster.

Substring match for event.type:error is unreliable

`_is_error_focused_query` checks whether `event.type:error` appears anywhere in the lowercased query string. It therefore matches negated queries such as `!event.type:error`, and queries with OR clauses that also include transactions. In those cases `sum(sample_weight)` runs over transaction rows, where the column doesn't exist or is null, producing wrong counts or query failures.

Trailing whitespace and misleading comments

Lines 223, 234 and 278 contain trailing whitespace, which lint will flag. The comments describing the check as a "cached result" and a "late transformation" for "query optimization" are inaccurate: the check simply runs on every call, and the transformation is the same in every branch.

sum(sample_weight) undercounts events lacking a weight

`upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` and assumes every event in an allowlisted project has one. Events with a null weight, such as those ingested before sampling was enabled, contribute 0 instead of 1. Wrapping the column as `ifNull(sample_weight, 1)` would count them correctly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error IDs zipped with nodestore results by position, can misattribute events

fetch_error_details zips `error_ids` with `events.values()` from nodestore get_multi. get_multi returns a dict keyed by node_id, and ordering or missing keys are not guaranteed to match the input list. Error details can therefore be attached to the wrong event id, or shifted when some ids are missing. Look up each result by its generated node_id instead of relying on position.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged table renders empty data

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization is passed hardcoded empty columns and empty data instead of `result`. Every table widget then renders blank for orgs with the flag on.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics recorded before feature check, and user id may be None

The assemble analytics event is recorded before the feature-flag check, so requests that are rejected with 404 are still counted. Under org-auth-token auth, request.user is anonymous and `request.user.id` is None.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

false_positives.candidate:
Replay query 'field' params passed to process_raw_response may drop error_ids

If the client sends `field` params, process_raw_response restricts the output to those fields. `error_ids` may then be missing, which silently disables error context.

Static method on CommitContextIntegration references PRCommentWorkflow

get_merged_pr_single_issue_template is defined on CommitContextIntegration but calls `PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title`. The helper is in the wrong class: the GitHub/GitLab PR comment workflows call `self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template` and `self.get_environment_info`. If these methods don't resolve on the workflow class, that call raises AttributeError.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is non-atomic (race allows reuse)

The backup code check reads user.backupCodes, nulls the matching entry in memory, then writes the array back with no compare-and-swap or transaction. Two concurrent logins with the same code both pass the check before either update lands, so one 'single-use' code can open multiple sessions. A concurrent use of a different code can also be overwritten by the last write, which revives a code that was already consumed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes screen can be dismissed without onEnable

On the DisplayBackupCodes step, 2FA is already enabled on the server. If the dialog is closed through onOpenChange (Escape key or overlay click) instead of the Close button, onEnable and resetState never run. The parent UI then shows 2FA as disabled while it is actually on. The step also stays at DisplayBackupCodes the next time the modal opens.

No tests for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The new authentication paths are untested: backup-code login, single-use enforcement, incorrect code, and disabling 2FA with a backup code. The PR leaves only a TODO comment for these cases.

Non-string backupCode in request body causes 500

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll` assumes a string. Any other truthy value (a number, an array) throws an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of a 400 validation error.

Unvalidated backupCode string can match nulled entries or throw

`credentials.backupCode.replaceAll` is called on raw input. Used codes are stored as `null`, so the check relies on indexOf of a string never matching null. That holds today, but the input is never validated for length or format. `replaceAll` also needs ES2021; on older runtimes this throws, and the user sees a generic error instead of a proper message.

formatBackupCode used before its const declaration

handleSetup calls `formatBackupCode`, which is declared later in the component body as a `const`. This only works because handleSetup runs asynchronously after render. It is fragile: an early call would throw a temporal dead zone error.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Crash when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` comes from destructuring `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`, so it is undefined whenever there is no destination calendar. The code then reads `.integration` on it without optional chaining. Any booking with Google Meet as location and no destination calendar throws a TypeError, which breaks booking creation. Use `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.

Fallback lookup compares against falsy externalCalendarId

This lookup only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy. It then searches for a calendar whose `externalId` equals that falsy value, which never matches. true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

Inverted slug condition for organization creation

The original code set `slug` only when team billing was disabled (`!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED`). The new code sets it only when billing is enabled. Self-hosted instances without billing now create orgs with no slug. Billing instances get a slug set immediately, even though they are meant to store it as `requestedSlug` until payment. This unrelated change reverses the intended behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

If the credential is neither in memory nor found in the DB (or has no app slug), `credential` is undefined and is still passed to `updateEvent`. `updateEvent` then reads `credential.appName` and throws, and the catch block marks every reference as failed. References whose credential is missing should be skipped instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Hangout patch uses undefined calendarId

`selectedCalendar` can now be undefined, in which case the insert falls back to "primary". The follow-up `events.patch` that adds the hangout link still passes `selectedCalendar` without that fallback, so the patch request fails. The patch should use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` value.

Only the first old calendar event is deleted when merging on reschedule

`updateAllCalendarEvents` now updates all calendar references. When `newBookingId` is set, however, it still deletes only `booking.references.find(...)`, i.e. the first old calendar event. The other hosts' old events are left orphaned in their calendars.

Organizer email taken from first destination calendar for every host's event

The organizer attendee email is always the first (main host's) destination calendar `externalId`. When the event is created in another host's calendar, the organizer email shown is the main host's calendar ID, not the organizer of that copy. This is inconsistent with the per-credential `selectedCalendar` used for the insert.

Recurring cancellation deletes are repeated per reference and only use the first calendar reference

The recurring-cancel branch now runs inside the loop over every calendar reference. Each iteration iterates all of the organizer's credentials and deletes only the first `_calendar` reference of each updated booking. With several hosts, the same deletes run N times and the other hosts' events are never deleted. In addition, those deleted results are pushed into `apiDeletes` after they have already been awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Overwrites missing refresh_token with literal placeholder

When the response has no refresh_token, it is set to the string "refresh_token". That placeholder gets persisted to the DB as the credential's refresh token, so later refreshes against the real provider fail. Separately, office365 previously tolerated parse failures, but the function now throws on them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Bogus zod schema keys

`[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the literal key "[object Object]". Both computed keys collapse to that same string, so the schema actually requires a property named "[object Object]". The intent was to accept any numeric expiry field, but in sync mode valid responses fail validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential key saved as safeParse result wrapper

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod SafeParseReturn object `{success, data}`, not the parsed data. Before this change the code stored the output of `googleCredentialSchema.parse`. Now the whole wrapper is written to credential.key, so the stored credential becomes `{success: true, data: {...}}`. credentialId passed as userId

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

Sync endpoint call unauthenticated, unchecked

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends no secret header, so the self-hoster's endpoint cannot verify the caller and anyone can request user tokens from it. The response status is also never checked, so error responses are treated as token payloads.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add arbitrary guests and trigger emails

Any authenticated user whose email matches an attendee can add unlimited new guests. Each addition sends emails from the organizer's name to arbitrary addresses and adds them to the organizer's calendar event. The guest list size is also unbounded, so this can be abused for spam.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

updateMany with empty data likely doesn't bump updatedAt

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError

When the credential is not found or belongs to another user, the handler throws a generic Error. tRPC turns this into a 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR rather than a NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN response, so clients cannot tell an access denial from a server failure. true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date formatting hardcoded to en-US

Cache status includes expired rows and runs even when caching is disabled

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

immediateDelete path never deletes the DB reminder row

When immediateDelete is true, the function cancels the batch at SendGrid and returns without deleting the workflowReminder row. On reschedule, the old reminders therefore stay in the database. Unscheduled reminders (scheduled=false) will later be picked up by the cron and sent for the old booking time. Each cancellation also adds a pending entry to SendGrid's scheduled_sends, which is capped at 100, so this path brings back the limit the PR is meant to avoid.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancelled reminders already past their date are deleted before cancellation runs

The deleteMany at the top runs first and removes rows whose scheduledDate is already past. A cancelled reminder whose date fell between cron runs (the cron runs every 15 minutes) is deleted without ever being cancelled at SendGrid. The email is then sent.

Cron still schedules reminders already marked cancelled

The query for unscheduled reminders does not filter out cancelled=true. A reminder for a cancelled booking that has no referenceId yet will be scheduled with SendGrid and sent. The cancel step only handles reminders scheduled within the next hour, and by then the email has already been queued.

One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the whole batch

The loop over cancelled reminders sits inside a single try/catch. If any SendGrid request throws (for example because referenceId is null or the 100-pending limit is hit), the remaining reminders are skipped. The delete promises collected so far are also never awaited, so those rows stay in the database.

Workflow delete skips unscheduled reminders and leaves SendGrid cancels pending

Reminders are queried with scheduled=true only, and the email path uses immediateDelete, which does not remove the row. The cascade delete of the workflow cleans up the rows, but every scheduled email still triggers an immediate SendGrid cancel. Deleting a large workflow can therefore exhaust the 100 pending-cancellation limit the PR set out to avoid.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A failing app import becomes an unhandled rejection at load time

The import promises are created eagerly and nothing awaits most of them. If any single app module fails to load (missing env var, syntax error, etc.), its promise rejects with no handler. That produces an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process, even if that app is never used.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async) makes calendar deletions fire-and-forget

Calendar and video deletions now run inside an async forEach callback whose promise is ignored. Failures surface as unhandled rejections rather than being reported to the caller. The same pattern in vital and wipemycalother reschedule.ts also makes their surrounding try/catch ineffective. Use `await Promise.all(map(...))` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
All app modules still eagerly imported at module load

Each entry is `import("./x")`, which starts loading every app module as soon as the appStore module is evaluated. Nothing is lazy, so startup and bundle cost are not reduced and the PR's goal is not met. The entries should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, called on demand by consumers.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in `calendar` field

`getCalendar` is now async, so `calendar` in each returned item is a Promise rather than a Calendar or null. `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await it, but other callers of `getCalendarCredentials` that use `item.calendar` directly are not. Those callers will receive a Promise, which is always truthy, so null checks pass and method calls on it fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working hours end check uses slot start instead of slot end

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, so it is identical to `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check never accounts for the event length, and slots that run past the end of working hours are accepted. It should be computed from `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with ===, zero-length override check never matches

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares two distinct object references, so it is always false. A date override where start equals end (a day marked unavailable) is therefore not caught by this branch. Use `.isSame()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Any non-matching working-hours entry marks the slot unavailable

`workingHours.find` returns true as soon as one working-hours entry covering that weekday excludes the slot. Users with several ranges on the same day (e.g. 9-12 and 13-17) will have every slot rejected, because each slot falls outside at least one of the ranges. The check should be "not inside any entry" rather than "outside some entry".

Date-override day matching shifts by the negated offset and compares in UTC

The override start is shifted by the negative organizer UTC offset, but the slot's day is compared in UTC. Overrides near midnight in non-UTC zones are matched to the wrong day, so they can be applied to, or missed on, adjacent days.

Override existence skips busy/booking checks

When a slot falls on a day with a date override and inside it, the function returns true before evaluating `busy`. As a result, existing bookings and calendar events on override days are ignored, which allows double bookings.

Slot that ends past the override end is still allowed

Only `slotStartTime.isAfter(override end)` is rejected. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after the override end passes this check. Combined with the early `return true` when an override exists, this skips the busy-time checks and can produce bookable slots that overrun the override window.

KeyError if integration metadata lacks sender

Network errors from token exchange are unhandled

OAuth redirect URL query not URL-encoded

redirect_uri and the other parameters are inserted into the authorize URL by f-string, without urlencode. A redirect_uri with special characters, such as a query string or ports with paths, can be parsed incorrectly by GitHub. Build the query with urlencode.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

Default `queued` timestamp is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once, when the module is imported. Every AssignmentSource then shares the same stale timestamp. The fix is `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
datetime in task kwargs breaks JSON serialization and the cycle check

`to_dict()` uses `asdict`, so the payload contains a raw `datetime` in `queued`. Celery's JSON serializer either rejects it or turns it into a string. If it becomes a string, the frozen dataclass still accepts it at the worker, so the type is silently wrong. If serialization fails, the outbound task is never enqueued. The datetime should be converted to an ISO string or timestamp before enqueuing and parsed back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature changed but never used

`assignment_source` was added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature, but no caller passes it. Status-sync cycles are therefore not addressed, and the signature now disagrees with the subclasses.

New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to integrations that don't accept it

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)`. Concrete implementations (Jira, VSTS, GitHub, etc.) were not updated in this PR. Any implementation whose signature lacks `**kwargs` will raise TypeError, breaking outbound assignee sync for that provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. That leaves the abstract members unimplemented: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. When `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` for a `metric_alert_fire` detector, Python raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. Before this change the class was a concrete no-op handler, so this is a crash that did not exist previously.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test builds expected occurrence with wrong value for group_2

The expected occurrence for group_2 is built with value 6, but the data packet supplies 10 for group_2. The tests pass only because the mock `build_occurrence_and_event_data` ignores `value`. As a result, nothing verifies that the hook receives the correct per-group value. The same pattern appears in other tests that use 6 for inputs of 8, 100 and 10.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

false_positives.candidate:
DetectorPriorityLevel converted to PriorityLevel without validation

`PriorityLevel(new_status)` assumes every `DetectorPriorityLevel` value has a matching value in `PriorityLevel`. Any non-OK detector level that does not map (for example a level added only to `DetectorPriorityLevel`) raises `ValueError` mid-evaluation. Because the dedupe update has already been enqueued at that point, the failure leaves enqueued state for that packet that is not consistent with what was actually processed. false_negatives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed names from mark_failed module break existing imports/mocks

Three names were removed from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`: `mark_failed_threshold` and `create_issue_platform_occurrence` were renamed and moved, and `get_failure_reason` was moved without a rename.

Patches on `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.produce_occurrence_to_kafka`-style paths will also stop intercepting calls, because that logic now lives in `incident_occurrence`.

Either update the callers and patch targets, or keep backward-compatible aliases in `mark_failed`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag name 'shards' vs 'shard'

The `wait_produce` timer is tagged `shards`, while the other new metrics use `shard`. Dashboards that filter by one tag name will miss this metric.

Separately, a comma-joined list of shards as a tag value increases cardinality and makes per-shard aggregation awkward.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process misses SpawnProcess

Processes are created with `mp_context.Process`, which produces `SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` is a subclass of `BaseProcess`, not of `multiprocessing.Process`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False.

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, hung flusher processes are therefore never killed. A replacement is spawned alongside them, leaving duplicate flushers on the same shards.

The same check in `join()` (line 346) means processes are never terminated on shutdown. Check against `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess` or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join breaks early on deadline, skipping termination of remaining processes

When the deadline is reached, the loop does `break` instead of continuing. Every remaining process is then left running without `terminate()` being called. These can keep flushing after the consumer is torn down or rebalanced, so the processes leak.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead code: _create_process_for_shard unused

`_create_process_for_shard` is never called anywhere, so it is dead code.

Zero assigned shards causes modulo/zero-process issues

If `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty (for example, an empty partition assignment during a rebalance), `num_processes` becomes 0. No flusher process is created, and `i % self.num_processes` would raise ZeroDivisionError.

A negative `--flusher-processes` value produces the same failure. Guard with `max(1, ...)` and validate the option.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from background thread

`_commit_loop` calls `commit_function` from a separate daemon thread. Arroyo's `Commit` callable is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the main thread, typically inside `poll()`/`submit()`. Calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's own loop can race on its internal state. Committable offsets should be computed and committed inside `poll()` instead.

Offset tracker state leaks across revoked partitions

Offsets for revoked partitions are never cleared from the tracker. If a partition is reassigned later, the stale `last_committed`/`all_offsets` state remains. A rewind to a lower offset would then never be committed, and stale entries for other partitions can still be committed after they are revoked.

Shared queue pool shut down on partition revocation

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once per factory and shared by every strategy that `create_with_partitions` returns. On a rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, which shuts down the shared pool's queues and workers. The next strategy then reuses that dead pool, and any `put` on it raises `ShutDown`. The consumer stops processing after the first rebalance.

Unbounded queues, no backpressure

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The docstring claims natural backpressure, but a slow worker lets memory grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling.

join() drops in-flight work and its final commit

`join()` sets the shutdown event and stops the commit thread before the queues are drained. Each worker's `shutdown` flag is also set, so the `while not self.shutdown` loop exits after the current item even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` alone would let it drain. As a result, queued items may never be processed, and offsets that were completed are never committed. After a rebalance this causes reprocessing, and work can be lost if another consumer has already committed past those offsets. The `timeout` argument is also ignored.

queue.ShutDown requires Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` only exist in Python 3.13 and later. On older interpreters the `except queue.ShutDown` clause raises `AttributeError` when it is evaluated, and `shutdown()` fails; the exception is caught and only logged. Workers then block in `get()` forever.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cached-permission miss always triggers full DB refetch, including for genuinely denied requests on fresh entries

Any cached negative result now bypasses the cache and queries the DB, through singleflight but still per request. This lasts until the denial cache absorbs it. For list-like access patterns with many distinct names the denial keys never repeat, so every denied Check costs a DB round trip. Cache hit metrics are also double-counted: a miss is recorded after a cache hit that did not allow.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key collides with permission cache key namespace

`userPermDenialCacheKey` builds keys with the same `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix as `userPermCacheKey` and joins parts with `_`. UIDs and folder names can themselves contain `_`, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key. A denial for one resource can then be applied to another. The two typed caches also share one store, and a key from one can be read by the other and fail to unmarshal. Use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous separator.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache defeats the purpose of fresh requery for newly created resources

When the DB requery still returns no grant, a denial is cached for 30s. Permissions for a newly created dashboard or folder can be written after the first Check, for example when the frontend checks before the creator's grant is persisted. In that case every later Check short-circuits on the denial key and never reaches the DB. The creator stays locked out for up to the TTL, which is the bug this PR is meant to fix. Nothing invalidates the denial key when permissions change.

Denial key uses raw subject UID, not resolved identifier; anonymous/renderer share keys

The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` as supplied, which may be a numeric ID or a UID, so one user gets inconsistent keys. Every anonymous subject also maps to one key. The renderer path's denials are cached as well, even though they are static. The permission cache uses the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`, so the denial cache keys should match it.

In-proc client caching fully removed

The in-proc client now uses a NoopCache, so every authz check goes through the server path. That path does at least the GetUserIdentifiers and permCache lookups plus JSON unmarshal. The earlier 30s client cache may have been hiding a high volume of these calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in list

This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

Silence drawer never opens in list view

The list view now passes only `promRule`; `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined. AlertRuleMenu still shows 'Silence notifications' because canSilence is computed from promRule abilities. However, the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. Clicking Silence therefore does nothing.
